packet.headline_seed: Astronauts return to ISS after sheltering during air leak repair attempt
packet.description_seed: Russian attempt to repair tunnel area sparks safe-haven procedure for five other astronauts onboard.

what: Astronauts return to ISS after sheltering during air leak repair attempt

clean_source_blocks.text: Russian attempt to repair tunnel area sparks safe-haven procedure for five other astronauts onboard.

Astronauts have been told to return to the International Space Station (ISS) after sheltering in their spacecraft while repair works were carried out on new air leaks in the Russian segment of the station. The five crew members had been told to assume an "elevated safety posture" as two Russian cosmonauts attempted repairs on the Zvezda service module's transfer tunnel. Nasa said the segment had suffered from cracks and leaks "for some time" - our science correspondent Pallab Ghosh reports this is not the first time the station has had to deal with such a problem. Russia's Interfax news outlet reported Roscosmos as saying two leaks were identified and one has already been fixed. It added that the crew and the ISS onboard systems were also not in danger, according to reporting by Russia's Tass news agency.

Nasa spokeswoman Bethany Stevens said the structural repair works had been paused while measurements and data were being assessed, prompting the astronauts' being told to return to the station. We are now ending our live coverage, but you can read the latest in our news story here. The leak that has put the ISS crew on alert today is not new - it has been one of the most persistent and troubling problems in the station's history, and despite years of attempts, engineers have never fully solved it. The problem is in the PrK - a small tunnel that connects a docking port to the Russian Zvezda service module. Microscopic structural cracks in its walls have been slowly releasing air into the vacuum of space.

NASA briefly directed astronauts aboard the International Space Station to shelter in a docked SpaceX Dragon spacecraft on June 5, 2026, after an air leak in the station’s Russian segment worsened. The alert was later lifted, and the crew returned to planned operations after Roscosmos paused repair work and NASA determined there was no immediate danger. NASA issued the order directing five astronauts to move into the Crew Dragon spacecraft and prepare for a possible evacuation, reversing it about two hours later. The leak is in the Russian Zvezda service module, an area of the station that has had recurring pressure-loss problems for years. According to Roscosmos, two leaks were found during pressure checks. One was sealed with a hermetic compound, while work on the second was paused so engineers could review additional data.

[Lähde: BBC World]
Astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) were ordered to shelter in an attached spacecraft after the structure suddenly started leaking more air.

Five of the seven crew were directed to go into the docked SpaceX shuttle Dragon "Freedom" on Friday afternoon and were braced for a potential evacuation.

Meanwhile, two remaining personnel - a pair of Russian cosmonauts - attempted to repair a part of the Russian segment of the ISS, where the leaks had started increasing on Monday.

The repairs were paused and the crew ordered back onto the ISS by Nasa on Friday afternoon.

Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, Sophie Adenot and Andrey Fedyaev, who arrived on the ISS in February, had been sheltering on the docked ship, along with another astronaut Chris Williams.

They had been told to put on their spacesuits so they were ready to undock and return to Earth at short notice.

The Dragon effectively functions as a lifeboat - attached to the station but ready to detach the moment the order is given.

The trigger for the order was a worsening air leak in the transfer tunnel, known as PrK, leading to a section of the Russian segment of the station called the Zvezda service module.

Russian cosmonauts, station commander Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and flight engineer Sergei Mikaev, attempted to fix the problem. Their escape route was the separately docked Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft.

Retired Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield, who was a commander of the ISS in 2012, said it had always leaked around half a pound of pressure a day.

"When you have an area that's leaking a little more, you get up to a pound a day, maybe a pound a half or even two, then we hit a threshold where, okay, we've got to do something about this," he told BBC Newshour.

"You're always one breath away from having to take shelter somewhere if the station has a problem. It's just a matter of fact of living on board a spaceship."

It is not the first time the station has had to deal with this latest leak - the cracks responsible have persisted on and off for around six years.

However, following the arrival of a Russian cargo ship last month, the Russian space agency Roscosmos noticed a fresh slow pressure drop in the tunnel, prompting the decision to move beyond patchwork fixes and attempt a more extensive repair operation on Friday.

But it was the method they were planning to use that prompted the order to take shelter, according to news agency Reuters.

payload.title: ISS-aseman miehistö palasi aluksestaan korjaustöiden keskeydyttyä
payload.summary: Kansainvälisen avaruusaseman viisi miehistön jäsentä määrättiin hetkellisesti SpaceX:n Crew Dragon -alukseen Venäjän segmentissä pahentuneen ilmavuodon vuoksi. Hälytys purettiin, kun korjaustyö keskeytettiin ja välitöntä vaaraa ei todettu.
payload.content:
Kansainvälisellä avaruusasemalla viisi miehistön jäsentä on palannut aseman puolelle sen jälkeen, kun heidät oli ohjattu hetkellisesti telakoituneeseen SpaceX:n Crew Dragon -alukseen Venäjän segmentissä pahentuneen ilmavuodon vuoksi. Varotoimi liittyi korjausyritykseen Zvezda-huoltomoduulin tunnelialueella, jossa painehäviöitä ja rakenteellisia halkeamia on havaittu jo pitkään.

## Varotoimi kesti noin kaksi tuntia

NASA määräsi viisi astronauttia siirtymään Crew Dragoniin 5. kesäkuuta 2026 ja valmistautumaan mahdolliseen evakuointiin. Määräys purettiin noin kahden tunnin kuluttua, minkä jälkeen miehistö sai palata suunniteltuihin tehtäviinsä avaruusasemalla.

Tilanne syntyi, kun kaksi venäläistä kosmonauttia yritti korjata vuotoja aseman Venäjän osassa. Miehistölle annettiin korotettu turvallisuusvalmius, mutta myöhemmin todettiin, ettei miehistöllä tai aseman järjestelmillä ollut välitöntä vaaraa. Korjaustyöt keskeytettiin, jotta mittauksia ja kerättyä dataa voidaan arvioida. NASA:n tiedottajan Bethany Stevensin mukaan rakenteelliset korjaustyöt pantiin tauolle arvioinnin ajaksi, ja tämän jälkeen astronautit ohjattiin takaisin asemalle.

## Vuoto liittyy PrK-tunneliin

Vuoto sijaitsee Zvezda-huoltomoduulin yhteydessä olevassa PrK-tunnelissa, joka yhdistää telakointiportin moduuliin. Alueella on ollut toistuvia painehäviöihin liittyviä ongelmia vuosien ajan. Lähdetietojen mukaan kyse on mikroskooppisista rakenteellisista halkeamista, joiden kautta ilmaa pääsee hitaasti avaruuden tyhjiöön.

Roscosmosin mukaan painekokeissa tunnistettiin kaksi vuotoa. Niistä toinen saatiin suljettua tiivistävällä aineella, mutta toisen korjaus jätettiin kesken lisäselvitysten ajaksi. Interfaxin ja Tassiin viitanneiden tietojen mukaan miehistö ja aseman järjestelmät eivät olleet vaarassa.

## Korjauksia jatketaan datan perusteella

Seuraava vaihe riippuu mittausten ja lisädatan arvioinnista. Tapaus liittyy alueeseen, jota insinöörit ovat yrittäneet korjata useiden vuosien ajan, mutta ongelmaa ei ole saatu pysyvästi ratkaistua. Tällä kertaa varotoimi jäi lyhyeksi, ja miehistö palasi normaaleihin toimintoihin korjaustyön keskeyttämisen jälkeen.
summary_bullets: Viisi ISS-aseman miehistön jäsentä määrättiin hetkellisesti Crew Dragon -alukseen Venäjän segmentin ilmavuodon vuoksi.
Hälytys purettiin noin kahden tunnin kuluttua, eikä miehistölle tai aseman järjestelmille todettu välitöntä vaaraa.
Vuoto liittyy Zvezda-huoltomoduulin PrK-tunneliin, jossa on ollut painehäviöongelmia jo vuosia.
